1240.title: The traditional middle
1240.hook: many Jews keep Shabbat dinner and festivals without full observance
1240.howItsDone: Traditional Jews may light Shabbat candles, make kiddush and share Friday night dinner, celebrate the festivals and keep family customs, while not keeping every law of Shabbat or kashrut.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Israeli categories, and your line: hiloni, masorti, dati, four words Israelis choose to describe how they live. Today, the middle word, and the people who live in it, in Israel and beyond.

A silver cup, a little dented, that belonged to a grandfather. Every Friday night it comes down from the shelf. The candles are lit, the blessing over the wine is sung in the grandfather's tune, the bread is torn and salted, and the family eats together with the phones in another room. Saturday morning, the same family gets in the car and drives to a soccer game. Nobody in the house sees a contradiction. They see a family that keeps what it has been handed. That way of living, kept by Jews in Israel and far beyond it, is today's word.
screen: `A DENTED SILVER CUP.` → `FRIDAY NIGHT, KEPT.` → `SATURDAY, THE SOCCER GAME.`

segments.voice: The traditional middle. It starts with a chain. Avot, the Mishnah's sayings of the fathers, opens with one: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, and onward, hand to hand. A traditional Jew stands in that chain and keeps holding on. Next, two words for Shabbat. In Exodus the commandment says, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy it says, "Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it." Tradition says both words, remember and keep, were spoken in a single utterance, and the Friday night song Lecha Dodi sings exactly that. Then, how the middle lives. Some Jews light the candles, bless the wine and bread, gather for the meal, sit at the seder, fast on Yom Kippur, and do not keep every law of the day. Observant Jews hold that remember and keep belong together and are meant to be lived together. Some traditional Jews describe what they do as holding on to what they can carry, out of love and loyalty. This lesson does not need to grade either. It only notes that the cup comes down every week. A middle is easy to overlook, because it has no movement and no manifesto. But in some families it is the hinge between generations: the grandfather's tune reaches the granddaughter because someone in the middle kept singing it.

segments.voice: Pick one tradition you keep, or someone you love keeps, partly: a holiday meal, a song, a blessing said on some nights and not others. Leave aside everything that isn't kept and look only at what is; feel its weight, the way a dented cup feels in the hand, and notice who handed it to you and who might receive it next. Then set it down gently, the way the cup goes back on the shelf.
The traditional middle. Jews who keep Shabbat dinner, the festivals and the family customs without keeping every law, holding on to what has been handed down. Today's word.
Your line: traditional. Held on to with love, and handed on. I'll be here tomorrow.

1241.title: No label
1241.hook: many Jews today choose no movement at all
1241.howItsDone: Jews who choose no movement may attend different synagogues for different occasions, study and celebrate with friends, keep customs at home, and describe themselves as just Jewish.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: traditional. The Friday night cup and the festivals, held on to and handed down. Today, Jews who skip the label altogether.

A registration form for a Jewish summer camp. Name, age, allergies. Then a row of little boxes: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, Other. A parent sits with the pen above the boxes for a long moment. The family lights candles most Fridays, goes to a different synagogue depending on who invites them, fasts on Yom Kippur, argues about Israel at dinner, and sends the kids to Hebrew school. None of the boxes fits. The parent ticks Other and writes, in small letters, just Jewish.
screen: `A ROW OF LITTLE BOXES.` → `NONE OF THEM FITS.` → `JUST JEWISH.`

segments.voice: No label. Go back to the people before the boxes. When the Israelites leave Egypt, the Torah says, "a mixed multitude went up also with them." There were no movement names on that road. The streams in this block, from Orthodox to Humanistic, are real and serious, and they are also newer than the people. Then the covenant. Moses tells the people in Deuteronomy, "Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath," but also with those standing there and those not there that day. In that reading, the covenant comes before any membership list. Now the shape of a no-label life. Some Jews today belong to no movement at all. They may pray at an Orthodox synagogue on the High Holy Days, take a class at a Reform temple, join a friend's Shabbat dinner, and keep their own customs at home. Some call themselves just Jewish. Some are simply not interested in the question. Each of the movements would say it offers something a person shouldn't do without: a community, a teacher, a framework that holds when life gets hard. That is a fair point, and a no-label Jew may well agree and still not pick a box. Last, a line for balance. Hillel taught, in the Mishnah, do not separate yourself from the community. No label is not the same as no people. A Jew without a movement can still be counted, still be welcomed, still belong. The label is optional. The belonging, in Hillel's view, is not.

1242.title: Lay-led communities
1242.hook: independent minyanim, where members lead prayer themselves
1242.howItsDone: In independent minyanim, members take turns leading prayer, reading from the Torah and giving short teachings, and members share the practical work of setting up, hosting and cleaning up.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: no label needed: some Jews choose no movement and simply describe what they do. On day seventeen you met the minyan, ten people praying together. Today, the rooms where those ten lead themselves.

A woman in a sweater gets up from a folding chair and begins the morning prayers. It's a rented room above a bookshop. A borrowed Torah scroll waits in a cabinet, beside a box of prayer books someone carried up the stairs. There's no rabbi on a stage, because there is no stage. Later a teenager reads from the Torah, nervous, carefully prepared. A retired dentist gives a five-minute thought on the week's portion. Next week, three different people will do those jobs. Groups like this go by a plain name: an independent minyan.
screen: `A WOMAN IN A SWEATER LEADS.` → `NO STAGE, NO PULPIT.` → `MEMBERS TAKE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Lay-led communities. Four turns. First, the quorum. A minyan is the group Jewish law asks for when a community prays together; the Mishnah lists prayers that are not said with fewer than ten. Streams differ on who counts toward the ten. What the law asks for is people, not a building and not a title. Second, the leader is a role, not a rank: the shaliach tzibbur, the messenger of the congregation. Jewish law does not require a rabbi for that job. Any member who knows the prayers can carry the room's words for a while, then sit back down. Third, the old picture behind it. At Sinai, the Torah says, God told the whole people: "ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." Readers hear many things in that line. Some in lay-led groups hear a job description: the holiness belongs to everyone in the room, so the work can too. Fourth, the cost. Nobody is paid to do it, so somebody has to. Someone sets up the chairs, someone learns to chant a Torah portion, someone brings the food and stays to wash the cups. Independent minyanim vary a great deal: some egalitarian, some traditional, some in between. Some members also belong to a synagogue with a rabbi, and value both. What they share is the habit of handing the work around. A room like that exists because ordinary people decided to lead it.
screen: `THE LAW ASKS FOR PEOPLE.` · `A MESSENGER, NOT A RANK.` · `A KINGDOM OF PRIESTS.` · `SOMEONE SETS UP THE CHAIRS.` · then, large: `LAY-LED.`

If you pray, offer the job up as you breathe; if not, just hold the picture steady.

1243.title: Shared ethics
1243.hook: every stream teaches giving, kindness and justice
1243.howItsDone: Jewish homes and synagogues in different streams keep tzedakah boxes, collect for the poor before holidays, and run volunteer projects; giving is described as justice, not only generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: lay-led, rooms where members take turns as the messenger of the congregation. You met tzedakah on day sixteen. Today it has company: what the streams hold in common when they act.

Two families on the same street could argue for an hour about Shabbat, or prayer, or who counts in a minyan. One keeps every detail of Jewish law; the other keeps almost none. Yet on both kitchen windowsills sits the same small tin box with a slot in the lid. Coins go in before candles are lit on Friday, or when a child finds a quarter in the couch. The box doesn't argue. It just fills up. Today is about the ground the streams stand on together, and the box is a good place to start.
screen: `TWO FAMILIES, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `THE SAME TIN BOX.` → `THE BOX DOESN'T ARGUE.`

segments.voice: Shared ethics. Three words, and one ladder. First, tzedakah, the giving that fills the box. It's usually translated charity, but some teachers hear in it tzedek, justice: giving is not a favor to the poor, it is part of setting the world right. Second, chesed, kindness beyond what anyone owes. Simeon the Just, in the Mishnah, says the world stands on three things: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness. Third, justice itself. The Torah doubles the word, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." And the prophet Micah gathers all three into one line: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Now the ladder. Maimonides, in his code of law, ranked ways of giving. Giving grudgingly sits low. Giving so that neither side knows the other sits high. At the top: helping someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they never need to ask again. Here's what makes this shared. These lines live in the Torah, the Prophets and the rabbinic books, the shelf the streams of this block read and argue over. Orthodox and Reform Jews may disagree about why a command binds. A Humanistic Jew may read Micah without a God who requires anything. The box still gets filled, and the soup still gets carried to the neighbor.

1244.title: Disagreeing with love
1244.hook: streams disagree on practice, conversion and marriage, and still share one people
1244.howItsDone: Jewish study is built on recorded disagreement: the Talmud preserves minority views beside the law, and study partners are expected to argue hard while learning each other's reasoning.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: shared ethics: giving, kindness and justice, from texts the streams read together. You heard these and these on day two hundred eighty-two. Today it goes to work, on the harder half: what happens when the streams don't agree.

Two schools of teachers, the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, disagree. Not once: over and over, on law after law. In the Talmud's telling, each house insisted the law followed them, and the argument would not end. Then a voice came from heaven and settled it. But listen to how. The voice did not say one side was right and the other wrong. It said something stranger, and the rabbis kept the sentence.
screen: `SHAMMAI AND HILLEL.` → `A VOICE FROM HEAVEN.` → `NOT RIGHT AND WRONG.`

segments.voice: Disagreeing with love. Four turns. First, the voice. In the Talmud's telling, it said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the House of Hillel. Both views are words of the living God; one still becomes the practice. Second, why Hillel. The Talmud asks that itself, and answers: Hillel's students were gentle and humble. They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even said Shammai's first. They won the law by the way they held the argument. Third, the test. The Mishnah says a dispute for the sake of heaven will last, and one that isn't, won't. Its example of the first kind is Hillel and Shammai. Its example of the second is Korah and his company, who rose against Moses for power. The question isn't whether people argue. It's what the argument is for. Fourth, the families. The two houses disagreed even about laws of marriage, which could have split them into two peoples. Yet the Talmud reports they did not refrain from marrying into each other's families. Today the streams disagree on real things: how to keep Shabbat, how a person converts, whose conversion counts, which marriages a rabbi will perform. Those disputes can wound, and love doesn't mean pretending they don't matter. The old model offers something narrower and harder: say the other side's view first, say it well, and keep the families at one table.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you disagree with about something that matters; not your worst fight, just one you can carry for two minutes. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer before you let them go.
Disagreeing with love. Holding a real dispute for the sake of heaven: stating the other view first and fairly, and staying one family. Today's word.

1245.title: The whole people
1245.hook: the Jewish people as one, beyond every movement
1245.howItsDone: Jews speak of klal Yisrael when they act for the Jewish people as a whole: supporting Jews in other countries, keeping practices that let others join them, and praying for Jews they will never meet.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: disagree with love: Hillel's students said the other side's view first. Today, the people all those arguments happen inside.

"And all the people answered together." That's the book of Exodus, at the foot of Mount Sinai. A crowd of former slaves, tired, unsure, some of them already complaining, and the text says they answered together. Not the elders for them. Not the best of them. All. This block has counted streams: Orthodox and Haredi, Conservative and Reform, Reconstructionist, Renewal, Humanistic, secular, traditional, no label at all. Today steps back far enough to see them as one thing.
screen: `ALL THE PEOPLE ANSWERED TOGETHER.` → `SO MANY STREAMS.` → `STEP BACK.`

segments.voice: Klal Yisrael. Klal means the whole, the general, everything together. Yisrael is Israel, the people. The whole people. Four turns. First, the camp. Earlier in the same chapter: "there Israel camped before the mount." The medieval commentator Rashi noticed that the Hebrew verb is singular: Israel camped, as one, like one person with one heart. On other days in the desert they quarreled. At Sinai they camped as one. Second, the answer: "All that the LORD hath spoken we will do." The covenant is made with a people, not a club of the most devoted. Third, what the phrase does today. Klal Yisrael points at something wider than any movement: the Jew in a black hat and the Jew who hasn't been to synagogue in years, the Jews of Morocco and Ukraine, of Ethiopia and Ohio. The arguments of this block happen inside a family, not between strangers. Fourth, the pull it creates. Some Jews feel it as a reason to keep a practice, so that Jews elsewhere can eat at their table or count them in their prayer. Others feel it as a reason to show up when Jews far away are in trouble. Different streams draw different lines on many questions. Klal Yisrael is the circle drawn around all of the lines.
screen: `KLAL: THE WHOLE.` · `ISRAEL CAMPED, AS ONE.` · `A COVENANT WITH A PEOPLE.` · `A CIRCLE AROUND THE LINES.` · then, large: `KLAL YISRAEL.`

If you're not Jewish, picture someone in your own community who prays, votes or lives very differently from you. Hold them in mind without arguing, as part of the whole, and if you pray, include them in your prayer.
Klal Yisrael. The whole people of Israel, taken as one, wider than any movement, any country, any way of practicing. Today's word.

1246.title: Love of fellow Jews
1246.hook: loving other Jews whatever their practice
1246.howItsDone: Jews speak of ahavat Yisrael when they help, host or pray for Jews unlike themselves, and teachers in several streams cite the Talmud's account of baseless hatred as a warning.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the whole people: Klal Yisrael, Israel camped as one at Sinai. Today, the feeling that holds the whole together, and the end of a week.

Why was the Second Temple destroyed? The Talmud asks it outright, and its answer is not about neglect. People then, it says, studied Torah. They kept the commandments. They did acts of kindness. What had gone wrong was between them: sinat chinam, hatred for no reason, Jew against Jew. The Talmud weighs that kind of hatred as heavy as idolatry, forbidden unions and bloodshed together. If baseless hatred can bring down a temple, the rabbis seem to ask, what holds one up?
screen: `WHY DID THE TEMPLE FALL?` → `NOT FOR LACK OF STUDY.` → `HATRED FOR NO REASON.`

segments.voice: Ahavat Yisrael. Love of Israel, love of one's fellow Jew. Four turns. First, the verse. Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Rabbi Akiva, in a teaching kept in the early commentary called the Sifra, called this a great principle of the Torah. Second, the verse right before it, easier to skip: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart." Not just: don't strike him, don't cheat him. Don't keep the hatred quietly inside. The Torah reaches into the place nobody else can see. Third, the cure. If baseless hatred tore something down, some teachers have said the repair must be its mirror image. Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook wrote of ahavat chinam, love for no reason: love that doesn't wait for the other person to practice the way you do, vote the way you do, or deserve it first. Fourth, the hard test. Loving Jews like you is the easy part. Ahavat Yisrael is tested by the Jew in the other stream, whose Shabbat you would never keep, whose politics you argue with. It doesn't erase the arguments. This week ran from the traditional middle, through no label and lay-led rooms, to shared ethics, disagreeing with love, and the whole people. Ahavat Yisrael keeps all of them in the same house.
screen: `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `DON'T HATE IN YOUR HEART.` · `LOVE FOR NO REASON.` · `THE TEST: THE JEW UNLIKE YOU.` · then, large: `AHAVAT YISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Find one divide in your own life: a cousin who practices differently, a neighbor across a political line, an old friend you stopped calling after an argument. Look for anything you've been holding against them quietly, the hating in the heart the verse means, and set it down for these two minutes; you don't have to fix it. Then picture one small step across, a message, a question, a kind word, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer.
Ahavat Yisrael. Love of one's fellow Jew, whatever their practice, rooted in the verse "love thy neighbour as thyself." Today's word.
Your line: love your fellow. Love for no reason doesn't wait to be earned. A week, complete.
